newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian bonds to enjoy brief reprieve.
newsitem.headline: Belgian bonds to enjoy brief reprieve.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures, bottoming out after the recent sell-off, will likely hold steady while awaiting direction from the U.S.

Dealers said players would monitor the U.S. market's reaction to the Treasury's quarterly refunding before deciding which way OLOs were headed. Meanwhile, speculation continued about Bundesbank measures to support the mark after the German central bank held its repo rate steady for another week.
"For OLOs there will be some recovery in the short term," an analyst said. "The market is pretty stable now after the impressive selling waves. It is time for some stabilisation."
"The unchanged repo rate exacerbated expectations about the next Bundesbank move...the bias is for curve flattening," another analyst said.
Short Belgian rates edged up amid the speculation.

One-week repo rates rose to 3.66/76 percent from 3.62/68 percent late on Monday and 3.55/65 percent late on Friday. By comparison, the rates are now almost 75 basis points above the central bank's central rate.
Kredietbank said it expected no rate moves until the early autumn with the Bundesbank holding off in anticipation of an improvement in the now weak German economy.
For now there was no reason for the Belgian central bank to act. "The franc is pretty stable, so the bank's policy will be unchanged," its analyst added.
Contrary to the expectations of some in the market, he did not expect the National Bank to be generous at today's weekly T-bill auction. The results are due at 1200 GMT.

Over 224 billion francs of bills expire today, triggering hopes that the bank might not soak up all of the cash returning to the market, thus injecting liquidity and pushing market yields down. One analyst said central banks, concerned about imported, dollar-driven, inflation, would keep credit tight.

"There is a commodity price explosion out there, making imported inflation worse...bonds have not priced this in," he said. Combined with the prospect of a pick-up in growth, this meant the upside scope for bonds was limited.
